steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
steps.body: More rain will probably fall in September than in July.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: In the past two years, significantly more rain has fallen in September than in July.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This isn't a crazy argument. The author is assuming that what happened in the recent past will probably happen again in the near future.

Given that September beat July in each of the last two years, how could we argue that July might still get more rain this year? Easily. Two years is a tiny record. Two seasons can line up that way by chance, the way a fair coin can land heads twice in a row. And maybe something about this year is different from the last two.

Notice that the author was careful: the conclusion says "probably," not "definitely." That softer wording helps, but it doesn't save the argument. Even "probably" needs more than two data points behind it. The flaw is the size of the record, not the strength of the claim.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the prediction rests on too few past cases: two years is not enough to say what this year will do. An answer could also say the author overlooks that this year may differ in some important way from the previous two. Expect abstract wording, so be ready to translate "future event" and "instances of related past events" back into this year's rain and the last two years.

notes.body: Circular reasoning means the premise already assumes the conclusion, so the argument proves nothing new. Here the premise is about the last two years and the conclusion is about this year. Those are different claims: the premise could be true and this year could still go the other way. The evidence is thin, but it is real evidence.

Translate the abstract words back into the argument. The phrase "an inference about a future event" is the prediction about this year's rain. The phrase "a very limited number of instances of related past events" is the two previous years. That matches our prediction exactly: two years is too small a record to support even a "probably" about this year.

The move to repeat: when an argument predicts the future from the past, count the past cases. If there are only a handful, look for an answer about a small or limited sample, often worded abstractly like this one.

The argument never mentions averages or one unusually wet year, so it can't overemphasize that possibility. It doesn't raise it at all. If anything, a critic would say the author ignores how one strange year could distort a two-year record. C describes the opposite of what the author does.

D describes concluding that two things are linked because they often show up together. The author doesn't conclude that anything is associated; the conclusion is a prediction about this year. And D's "many instances" gets the evidence backwards: the problem here is that there are only two.

The argument cites no source at all. The rainfall in the previous two years is stated as a premise, and on Flaw questions we accept premises as true. Even with perfect rainfall records, two years would still be too few, so reliability isn't the problem.

why: PT158 register: em dashes, padded 100+ word notes, outside weather facts in the B note, a gendered example and a typo in Evaluate, and wrong-answer notes without a test.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: There are exceptions to the general rule that people should practice what they preach. Rephrase: sometimes it's fine for people not to act the way they tell others to act.

steps.label: Evidence (for instance)
steps.body: Logicians don't need to be logical in their discussions of logic, any more than physicians need healthy lifestyles in order to treat people.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The author's example of an exception is an analogy. Physicians preach health, and nobody thinks a physician has to live a healthy life to treat patients well. So, says the author, logicians don't have to be logical in their discussions of logic either.

Any time an argument rests on an analogy, ask: are these two cases alike in the way that matters? The physician case works. A physician's lifestyle happens outside the job. A physician who never exercises can still diagnose and prescribe correctly.

The logician case is different. Being logical while discussing logic isn't something a logician does after work. It is the work. A logician who argues illogically about logic is doing the job badly. How would anyone come away understanding logic if the lesson itself were illogical?

So, given the physician example, how could we argue the logician example still fails? Point out that the physician's failure is personal, while the logician's failure is professional.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that breaks the analogy: being illogical in discussions of logic is a failure at the logician's actual job, while an unhealthy lifestyle doesn't stop a physician from treating people well. The stem says "fails to take into account," so the right answer will be a fact that, had the author considered it, would weaken the comparison.

notes.body:
This is the broken analogy we predicted. A logician who is illogical in discussions of logic is failing at the core of the job, which is incompetence. A physician with an unhealthy lifestyle can still treat people well. So the two cases aren't alike in the way the argument needs.

Run the stem's test. The phrase "fails to take into account" means ask whether the idea would weaken the argument. It does. If the logician's failure is incompetence and the physician's isn't, the physician example can't earn logicians the same pass.

The move to repeat: on an analogy argument, the right Flaw answer usually names the relevant difference between the two cases.

B is about a physician whose health "deteriorates badly," not one with an unhealthy lifestyle, which is what the argument discusses. And at most B questions the physician half of the analogy, which is the half that works. It says nothing about whether a logician must be logical when discussing logic.

The argument is about what each profession needs to do, not about which one causes more harm. Incompetent physicians could be far more dangerous than illogical logicians, and the question of whether logicians must be logical about logic would be untouched.

How hard a standard is to meet doesn't decide whether it is required. Something can be very difficult and still be necessary for doing a job well. D compares difficulty, while the argument is about necessity, so it misses the flaw.

E agrees with the author: it accepts that logicians don't need to be logical to be competent at discussing logic. Calling it "highly desirable" doesn't contradict the claim that it isn't necessary. A Flaw answer has to hurt the argument, and an answer that concedes the author's point can't be what the author failed to account for.

why: PT158 register notes (em dashes, 110+ word repetition); breakdown had gendered pronouns for the physician and logician, a garbled Conclusion rephrase, and an Evidence step that misquoted the physician half of the analogy.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: My paper wasn't graded in accordance with the professor's stated criteria.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The professor said A's would go only to papers whose conclusions were supported by reliable statistical evidence. My conclusions were supported by reliable statistical evidence, and the professor admits it, but my paper got a B.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
When a Flaw stimulus contains conditional logic, suspect the most common famous flaw: Necessary vs. Sufficient. The author takes a rule and runs it backward or negates it.

"Only" introduces a necessary condition. So the professor's rule is:

gets an A → conclusions supported by reliable statistical evidence

That rule says reliable evidence is required for an A. It doesn't say reliable evidence earns an A. The student reasons: my paper had reliable evidence, so it should have gotten an A. That is the reversal. It treats a requirement as a guarantee.

An everyday version: "Only people with a ticket get into the concert." Having a ticket doesn't promise entry. You could still be turned away for showing up after the doors close. The professor may have other requirements too, like clear writing or a sound argument, and the paper may have missed one of them. A B is perfectly consistent with the stated rule.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer calling out the formal Necessary vs. Sufficient error: the student treats something required for an A as if it were enough for an A. An answer could also say the student fails to consider that there may be other requirements for an A besides well-supported conclusions.

notes.body: A accuses the student of a motive: bringing up the criteria to distract from the paper's weaknesses. Nothing in the argument tells us why the student is complaining. The flaw is in how the student reads the rule, and that flaw would be there whatever the motive.

The conclusion is close to a factual claim: whether the grading matched the professor's stated rule. And even if we call it evaluative, arguing from facts to an evaluation isn't a flaw on its own; plenty of good arguments do it. The student's facts are fine. The error is reading "only" as if it meant "always."

This is the reversal we predicted, in abstract words. The phrase "a condition that is among the requirements for a particular grade" is reliable statistical evidence, which the word "only" makes required for an A. The phrase "a condition that is enough to guarantee that grade" is how the student treats it: I had reliable evidence, so I deserved an A.

The move to repeat: when a Flaw stimulus has "only," "only if," "requires," or "must," diagram it, then check which side the author treats as the trigger. If the author uses the necessary side to prove the sufficient side, the answer will say the argument confuses what is required with what is enough. The test can word that many ways: "necessary" vs. "sufficient," "required" vs. "guarantee," or, as here, "among the requirements" vs. "enough."

D says the argument rests on a biased report. But the key fact isn't the student's word alone: the professor acknowledges that the conclusions were supported by reliable statistical evidence. And a neutral observer making this exact argument would commit the same error, so bias isn't the flaw.

The student's conclusion is about the professor's stated criteria, not about some objective standard of quality. The argument never brings up objective criteria, so it has no need to distinguish them. The flaw is a misreading of the professor's own rule.

why: PT158 register notes (em dashes, padded); Evaluate had a typo, gendered pronouns for the student and professor, and a dating example; D and E notes missed the sharpest reasons (the professor's own acknowledgment; the conclusion is about stated criteria).

steps.label: Conclusion (clearly, then)
steps.body: The company acted fairly in failing to give bonuses to the staff.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Some people claim the company was unfair, perhaps because they recall that the company promised that if profits were higher than last year's, the staff would get bonuses.
But profits were much smaller than last year's.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Lindsey is rebutting an opposing position. Some people say the company was unfair. Lindsey guesses at their reason ("Perhaps"): the company's promise that the staff would all get bonuses if profits increased over last year's. Then Lindsey knocks that reason down. The promise was:

profits increase over last year's → staff all get bonuses

Profits were much smaller than last year's, so the promise never kicked in, and it didn't require bonuses. Fair enough. But Lindsey concludes much more: the company acted fairly.

Given that the promise didn't require bonuses, how could we argue the company still acted unfairly? Easily. Maybe the staff worked unpaid overtime all year. Maybe executives paid themselves large bonuses while the staff got nothing. The critics may have had reasons Lindsey never mentions.

This is the famous Unproven vs. Proven False flaw. Defeating one argument for a claim doesn't prove the claim false. Example: "Some people say this restaurant is bad, perhaps because the parking is terrible. But the lot was just doubled in size. Clearly the restaurant is good." The food could still be awful.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying Lindsey concludes a claim is false just because one possible reason for it fails. An answer might also point out that Lindsey only guesses at the critics' reason ("Perhaps") rather than answering the reasons they actually gave.

notes.body: Lindsey doesn't rely on the critics' opinions; Lindsey argues against them. Whether those unnamed people were well informed doesn't matter to the reasoning, because their view is never used as evidence. A describes building a case on someone's opinion, which is the reverse of what happens here.

This matches the prediction. In B, "an opinion" is the claim that the company was unfair. The phrase "one potential reason for that opinion" is the bonus promise, which Lindsey only guesses the critics had in mind. And "has been undermined" is the point that profits fell, so the promise never required bonuses. From that alone, Lindsey infers the opinion is false and the company was fair.

The word "merely" carries the criticism: one failed reason isn't enough to prove the opposite. The move to repeat: when an author attacks an opponent's reason and then concludes the opponent's claim is false, look for Unproven vs. Proven False. Showing that a reason fails leaves the claim unproven, not disproven.

C describes an attack on the people: dismissing a claim because of who made it. Lindsey says nothing about the critics' character, motives, or qualifications. Lindsey goes after a reason for their claim, the bonus promise, so the attack is on an argument, not on people.

D is tempting because the argument is about profits. But there's no confusion. The promise was about an increase over last year's profits, and Lindsey compares this year's profit to last year's, which is exactly the right comparison. A profit much smaller than last year's is not an increase. The math is fine; the error is the leap from one failed reason to the claim that the company acted fairly.

Run the test: "overlooks the possibility" means ask whether the idea would weaken the argument. E says a policy can be fair without being generous. That helps Lindsey, who argues the company was fair even though it paid no bonuses. An idea that supports the conclusion can't be what the author failed to consider.

why: PT158 register notes with em dashes and padding; the B and D notes misstated the critics' reason as large profits; Evaluate used gendered pronouns for Lindsey and never showed the promise was untriggered.

steps.label: Conclusion (probably)
steps.body: Making some stuff from recycled materials is probably as bad for the environment as it would be to make it from nonrecycled materials.

steps.label: Evidence (and)
steps.body: The recycling process for those products uses as much energy as producing them from raw materials, and almost all energy production damages the environment.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Given that recycling these products uses as much energy as producing them from raw materials, how can we argue that making them from recycled materials is still better for the environment?

One route would be to say the energy used for recycling is cleaner. The second premise mostly blocks that: almost all energy production damages the environment.

So look past energy. Energy is only one way that making a product can harm the environment. What about mining, logging, or drilling for the raw materials in the first place? What about the waste that goes to a landfill when nothing is recycled? Recycling could win on those counts even if energy is a tie.

The columnist treats one part of the environmental cost as if it were the whole cost. Two options that tie on one factor only tie overall if nothing else differs.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the columnist fails to consider environmental effects other than energy use. The best version would say recycling might help the environment in some way unrelated to energy. That would show the energy tie doesn't settle the overall comparison.

notes.body: Equivocation needs a key word to change meaning between premise and conclusion. Here "environment" means the same natural world throughout: energy production damages it, and making products damages it. The problem is that the columnist counts only one kind of damage, not that the word shifts.

B says the argument mixes up cause and effect. But the argument's only causal claim runs the normal way: energy production causes environmental damage. The columnist never treats the damage as a cause of energy use, so nothing is reversed.

C would fit if the columnist drew a conclusion about all recycled products from a few. But the conclusion is limited to "some types of products," the same products the premise is about ("those products"). The argument never generalizes, so representativeness isn't an issue.

This matches the prediction. The columnist compared the two options on one factor, energy, found a tie, and declared them tied overall. D names what got left out: making products from recycled materials "may have environmental benefits unrelated to energy consumption," such as less mining or logging, or less landfill waste.

Run the stem's test. The phrase "fails to consider" means ask whether the idea would weaken the argument. If recycling helps the environment in ways that have nothing to do with energy, then equal energy use doesn't make the two options equally damaging. The conclusion falls.

The move to repeat: when an argument compares two options on one factor and draws a conclusion about the whole, look for the answer naming another factor that could tip the balance.

E describes the post hoc flaw: one thing followed another, so the first caused the second. Nothing in the argument relies on timing or sequence. The claim that energy production damages the environment is stated as a general premise, and on Flaw questions we accept premises as true.

why: PT158 register notes (em dashes, 110+ words); the B and E notes misdescribed the argument's causal content; Goal used a gendered pronoun for the columnist and named the task more than the answer; Evidence misquoted the energy premise.

steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
steps.body: If we want there to be even fewer parking violations, the fines should be raised again.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Six months ago the city raised the fines for parking violations, to help pay for a parking garage that had just opened. Since then, parking violations on city streets have dropped by 50 percent.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
A common pattern in Logical Reasoning: "Policy X went into effect. Then Y happened. So X caused Y." The official assumes the higher fines caused the 50 percent drop. The conclusion depends on that causal story: "if we want there to be even fewer parking violations, the fines should be raised again" only makes sense if fines are what reduced violations.

This is an Explain Curious Fact argument. Curious fact: violations dropped by half. The official's explanation: the higher fines. Alternate explanation: read the first sentence again. A new parking garage opened at the same time. Drivers who used to park illegally on the street may now have somewhere legal to park. That would cut violations whether or not the fines changed.

The official mentions the garage only as the reason the fines were raised, then forgets about it. That's the detail the test wants us to catch. When a stimulus mentions a second change at the same time, ask whether that change could explain the result.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for an answer saying the official fails to rule out another cause for the drop. The best one names the obvious rival: the new garage gave drivers more legal places to park.

There's also a smaller worry. Even if the fines did cause the drop, raising them again may not add much. At some point the fine is already high enough: whether it's $500 or $600, I'm equally determined not to get that ticket. But the official only predicts "even fewer" violations, so this worry is weaker than the garage, which threatens the causal claim the whole recommendation rests on.

notes.body: A describes reversed causation: treating something that resulted from the drop as if it caused the drop. The fine increase came first, six months ago, and was made to help pay for the garage, not in response to fewer violations. Nothing here that came after the drop is being cast as its cause.

B is the most tempting wrong answer because it sounds like a real worry: maybe a second raise won't work as well. But check what the official needs. The conclusion only says raising fines again would bring "even fewer" violations. Any further drop would do. Negate B: a second raise reduces violations less than the first did. The conclusion can still be true, so the argument doesn't take B for granted.

Compare that with E. If the garage caused the drop, the fines may do nothing at all, and the recommendation collapses.

The city's income from fines has nothing to do with whether higher fines reduce violations. The conclusion is about getting fewer violations, and money the city earns can't weaken a claim about how fines change drivers' behavior.

The official doesn't need illegal parkers to prefer parking legally. A higher fine can push people into legal spaces they dislike. Negate D: illegal parkers would rather keep parking illegally. Fines could still deter them, so the argument survives, which means D isn't something it assumes.

This is the alternate cause we predicted. The garage opened at the same time the fines went up, so either change could explain the 50 percent drop. If the drop came from the new parking spaces, raising fines again may do nothing, and the recommendation falls apart.

The stem's wording, "fails to establish," means the argument needed this and didn't prove it. To recommend higher fines, the official had to rule out the garage, and didn't.

The move to repeat: when an argument credits one change for a result, scan the stimulus for anything else that changed at the same time. The rival cause is often planted in a clause that reads like background, like "to help pay for the parking garage that had just opened."

why: Breakdown never mentioned the new parking garage, which is the whole answer; PT158 register notes with em dashes; the B trap note didn't run the test (the conclusion only needs some further drop).

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
At one Tuesday meeting, the club's president took a survey of all members present.
Of those surveyed, 95 percent said that they had no difficulty attending on Tuesdays.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The club's president concluded that the attendance problem [at weekly meetings] was not due primarily to schedule conflicts.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Let's survey the customers at a sushi restaurant about whether they like fish. Or ask the people at a dog park whether dogs make good pets. We know what answer we'll get.

The president did the same thing. The survey went only to members present at a Tuesday meeting. Of course those people have no trouble attending on Tuesdays: they're there. The members most likely to have a Tuesday conflict are the ones who missed the meeting, and they never got a survey.

That matters because the attendance problem is about the people who don't come. The president drew a conclusion about why members miss meetings from the members who didn't miss this one. How many absent members stay home because Tuesday doesn't work for them? The survey can't tell us.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer describing a Sampling flaw: the president generalized from a sample that isn't representative of the group the conclusion is about. The answer might say it abstractly (an unrepresentative sample) or concretely (the survey left out members who couldn't attend on Tuesday).

notes.body: Circular reasoning means the premise already assumes the conclusion. Here the premise is a survey result and the conclusion is about why attendance is low. Those are different claims. The result was close to guaranteed by who was asked, which can feel circular, but that is a sampling problem, not a premise restating the conclusion.

This matches the prediction. In B, "a sample that is likely to be unrepresentative" is the members present at a Tuesday meeting. The phrase "making a generalization" is the conclusion about why the club has an attendance problem. The survey asked only the people who made it on a Tuesday whether Tuesday works for them, so the members with Tuesday conflicts were screened out by the way the survey was taken.

The move to repeat: whenever a conclusion rests on a survey, ask who got the survey and who didn't. If the method leaves out the very people the conclusion is about, the answer is a sampling flaw.

C is tempting because 95 percent is not 100 percent. But the president didn't treat the result as having no exceptions. The conclusion is that the problem was not due "primarily" to schedule conflicts, which allows for some conflicts. The flaw is who was surveyed, not how far the president stretched the number.

No two premises conflict. A survey was taken at a Tuesday meeting, and 95 percent of those surveyed had no difficulty attending on Tuesdays. Both can be true together. The premises are consistent; they just don't support the conclusion.

E describes a necessary vs. sufficient error about a change that won't solve a problem. The president never claims that moving the meeting wouldn't be enough to fix attendance and then infers it isn't needed. The argument runs from a survey to a conclusion about the cause, with no conditional reasoning at all.

why: Goal was one generic line; PT158 register notes with em dashes and padding; the A note misstated the president's conclusion; Evaluate had a typo; the C trap note missed that 'primarily' already allows exceptions.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: If the proposed measures are adopted, we'll spend about a billion dollars less on ozone-related health costs.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
If the proposed measures are adopted, ozone levels in the city's air will be one fifth lower than they are now.
Ozone is currently responsible for over $5 billion in health costs.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The author takes one fifth of the $5 billion in ozone health costs and assumes that cutting ozone by one fifth cuts those costs by one fifth.

But who said the relationship is one to one? Given that ozone will drop by a fifth, how could we argue the costs won't drop by a billion?

Maybe health costs depend on a threshold. Suppose ozone makes people sick only above a certain level, and even 80 percent of today's ozone is well above it. Then cutting ozone by a fifth might barely change health costs. Or it could run the other way: the last fifth of the ozone could be the most harmful part, and the savings could be bigger than a billion.

Either way, the argument needs costs to rise and fall in step with ozone levels, and it never shows that.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying "just because ozone is reduced by one fifth doesn't mean ozone-related health costs will be reduced by one fifth." In flaw language: the author presumes, without evidence, that health costs are proportional to ozone levels.

notes.body: Check the conclusion's exact words: we would spend less on "these ozone-related health costs." If other pollutants rose, other health costs would rise, not ozone-related ones. So A attacks a claim about total health costs that the author never made.

This names the assumption we predicted. The author got from $5 billion to about $1 billion by taking one fifth, which only works if ozone-related health costs vary "roughly in proportion to ozone levels." The argument offers no evidence for that. If costs only kick in above some threshold, a one fifth cut in ozone could save far less than a fifth of the costs.

Run the stem's test on a "presumes" answer: negate it and see if the argument survives. Health costs don't vary in proportion to ozone? Then the billion-dollar figure has no support. So the argument depends on B.

The move to repeat: when an argument turns a percentage change in one thing into the same percentage change in another, look for a proportionality assumption.

The conclusion is conditional: we would save the money "should the proposed measures be adopted." It never claims the measures will be adopted, so it owes us no reason to think they will be. C criticizes the argument for not proving something it never claimed.
The argument contains no appeal to emotion. It runs on numbers: a one fifth reduction, over $5 billion, about a billion. The flaw is in that math, not in an attempt to stir up feelings.

E accuses the author of a motive: using air pollution to distract from bigger health costs. Nothing in the argument suggests a hidden purpose. The topic is ozone-related costs, and the argument stays on it. The error is a bad assumption about those costs, not a change of subject.

why: Evidence step misstated the premise as ozone falling to one fifth (it falls by one fifth) and the Conclusion dropped 'ozone-related'; PT158 register notes with em dashes; the A note missed that the conclusion covers only ozone-related costs.
